name: Lotud
confidence_why: Blood and Blood 1993 and Blood and Blood 1994, the only descriptions of Lotud stress and both products of the same 1985-87 fieldwork in Tuaran, agree that stress falls by default on the penultimate syllable (first syllable in disyllables, second-from-last in trisyllables); the only qualification is their own list of exceptions, such as final stress on hilú' and kadái, level stress on closed-closed disyllables like pándán, first-plus-last stress on some trisyllables, and shifts under affixation (túmahak but tahákon), and no other source (Banker 1984, Lobel 2013, the 1987 word list, the 2023 dictionary) says anything about stress.

catalog_quote: [1994: 20] Two-syllable words are common in Lotud, and the most common pattern is stress on the first syllable. All of the two syllable words in this conversation have the stress on the first syllable with the exception of pándán, which has equal stress on both syllables. This is typical of words with two closed syllables, such as mántád from a previous conversation. However, there are other common words which are stressed on the last syllable, hilú’ and kadái, for example. Though this is the pattern for elicited words, in the context of a sentence the stress on a word may shift to the final syllable, for instance for emphasis. In three-syllable words the stress is most commonly on the second from the last syllable, as you will see in the words mamátuw, momónsoi, and kadáyan. Other three-syllable words regularly have stress on both the first and last syllables, the stronger stress often depending on the context of the word. From former conversations there are: ósomók, árahí, and kárabáu. Sometimes difference in affixation changes the stress. We find túmahak but also tahákon. Another variant of o and a occurs in unstressed syllables in words of three syllables or more: o or a in that unstressed part of the word becomes a schwa: kárabáu kíkarája’ nókoórom bórosón nóko’údan ... [1993: 59] Stress is noncontrastive.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The authors state only that stress is not contrastive; the pages available (59-62) give no placement rule. Their stress-marked phonetic forms show penultimate stress in every disyllable and, in words of three or more syllables, primary stress on either the penult ([tu'tubit], [kə'dayən], [mə'ŋaki], [ʔi'nɔwit], [ˌnɔkə'siŋud], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ]) or the final syllable ([mɔgi'hum], [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌʔantə'dan], [ˌʔɔsə'mɔk], [ˌbino'kol], [ˌʔiŋgarə'nan]), i.e. a right-edge (penult~final) stress whose conditioning is not stated in the accessible pages; pp. 63-69 of the article (not scanned) may contain the rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in the available pages, but transcriptions mark a secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of three or more syllables (e.g. [ˌnatə'nan], [ˌmamə'naw], [ˌnɔkə'siŋud], [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ], [ˌʔiŋgarə'nan]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; unassimilated Malay loans keep Malay shape ([pər'tʃuma] 'free', ['tʃukup] 'enough'). Vowel reduction of /a/, /ɔ/ to [ə] is tied to unstressed syllables (p. 62).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (isolated words elicited 1985-87 in Kg. Ro'un, Damat and Tutu, 'main dialect' of Lotud); no phrase-level discussion in the pages seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Blood & Blood 1993 describe what they call the 'main dialect' of Lotud (Kg. Ro'un, Damat and Tutu near Tuaran; also known as Dusun Tuaran) = Glottolog lotu1250, ISO dtr. Banker 1984 notes a second dialect, 'Dusun Kadayan' of Telipok/Sumagit, not covered by the phonemics paper. Lobel 2013 places Lotud in a Bisaya-Lotud subgroup rather than Dusunic proper.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog penultimate stress (initial on disyllables, penult on trisyllables) is exactly the 'most common pattern' this work states, so placement agrees. It adds what the catalog and Blood & Blood 1993 (existing statement: 'Stress is noncontrastive', stress-marked forms pp. 60-62) lack: level stress on closed-closed disyllables, lexically final-stressed words, first+last stress on some trisyllables (which matches the 1993 forms with initial secondary stress and final primary such as [ˌʔɔsə'mɔk] = 1994 ósomók), affixation-conditioned shift, phrasal emphasis shift, and schwa reduction of unstressed o/a. It sits in mild tension with the 1993 'noncontrastive' label, since final-stressed hilú’…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable, trisyllables 'most commonly on the second from the last syllable' (mamátuw, momónsoi, kadáyan). Exceptions: disyllables with two closed syllables carry equal stress on both (pándán, mántád); some common words are stressed on the final syllable (hilú’, kadái); some trisyllables carry stress on both first and last syllables with the stronger one depending on context (ósomók, árahí, kárabáu); affixation can move the stress (túmahak vs tahákon); in sentence context stress 'may shift to the final syllable, for instance for emphasis'. Unstressed o/a reduce to schwa in words of three or more syllables (kárabáu, kíkarája’, nókoórom, bórosón, nóko’údan).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as 'secondary'. p. 20: some trisyllables 'regularly have stress on both the first and last syllables, the stronger stress often depending on the context of the word' (ósomók, árahí, kárabáu). p. 38: 'Reduplicated words are pronounced as if they were one word.. Ambat-ambat from this conversation is pronounced ámbatámbat.'
new_statements.exceptions: Level stress on disyllables with two closed syllables (pándán, mántád); lexically final-stressed words (hilú’, kadái); first+last stress on some trisyllables; affix-conditioned shift (túmahak / tahákon); phrasal emphasis shift to the final syllable (p. 20). The statement covers only elicited words: 'Though this is the pattern for elicited words, in the context of a sentence the stress on a word may shift to the final syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: The Conversations describe the 'Lotud Dusun language' as studied 'in two different villages in the Tuaran district' (p. iii); no named dialect (Webonary lists Suang Lotud, Suang Olung, Suang Sarayoh and Dusun Kadayan as Lotud dialects). Same authors and presumably the same variety as the 1993 phonemics already in the catalog.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on placement: Blood & Blood 1993 ('Stress is noncontrastive'; phonetic forms mostly penult, some trisyllables final with initial secondary) and Blood & Blood 1994 (disyllables first-syllable, trisyllables 'second from the last' as the most common pattern) both support penultimate default, which is the catalog's penultimate stress. The only tension is in the type label: 1993 calls stress noncontrastive, whereas 1994 lists common words with final stress (hilú’, kadái) beside the initial-stress default and an affix-conditioned shift (túmahak vs tahákon), which makes placement partly lexical or morphological rather than fully predictable; 1994 gives no minimal pairs, so 'noncontrastive' and 'penult default with exceptions' are compatible readings of the same facts. 1994 also adds level stress on closed-closed disyllables (pándán, mántád), which 1993's marked forms neither show nor exclude (its disyllables with closed final syllables such as ['sakɔt̪], ['sisip] have open first syllables).
